citation.title: Chocolate Scents and Product Sales: A Randomized Controlled Trial in a Canadian Bookstore and Cafe

standing_assumptions:
The article (SpringerPlus (2016) 5:670, DOI 10.1186/s40064-016-2303-5; six pages; the first page is unnumbered and the others are headed ‘Page 2 of 6’ to ‘Page 6 of 6’, so the printed page number equals the PDF page number) is an empirical report of one randomized field experiment. It states no theorem, proposition, lemma or corollary, displays no formula and gives no proof; its statistical statements are made in running text and in Table 1. Everything quoted from the article below was read from the page images.
(S1) Design. Methods, p. 2 (PDF p. 2): “We conducted a trial over 31 days in an 800-square-foot independent bookstore in Canada.” p. 3 (PDF p. 3), left column: “The trial used a between-subjects design in which the 31 experimental days were assigned one of two conditions: chocolate scent dispersion (treatment) and no scent (control). Condition was determined by Bernoulli (coin flip) random assignment with probability .5 independently across days.”
(S2) Outcomes. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), left column: “Sales data were recorded in three categories: book sales, café sales (pastries, coffee, and tea), and bulk sales (primarily coffee beans, but also loose tea and spices).”
(S3) The manipulation check. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), right column, first paragraph of ‘Results and discussion’: “A manipulation check modeled after Doucé et al. was conducted to evaluate four aspects of the scent: spontaneous detection, prompted detection, spontaneous identification, and recognition of the scent. Fifteen customers were asked to respond to questions about the store atmosphere. To assess spontaneous detection, customers were asked whether they noticed something special in the store atmosphere, with responses coded as 1 if the customer mentioned an ambient scent, 0 otherwise. If the customer did not volunteer that a scent was present, ambient scent was mentioned and the subject was asked whether they could detect a scent now that scent was mentioned. Subjects were then asked if they could identify the scent. Subjects who did not spontaneously identify the scent as chocolate were asked if they recognized the scent as chocolate.” Second paragraph, last sentence: “Our objective was to maintain a detectable ambient scent; we did not seek to eliminate spontaneous detection of the chocolate scent.” The third paragraph is the passage of finding P040-E001 and is transcribed in full in P040-T3. The article names no method for its interval, gives no formula for it and describes no sampling scheme for the fifteen customers.
(S4) The two regression analyses. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), right column, last lines, continuing on p. 4 (PDF p. 4), left column: “We present two regression-based analyses of the trial. The first is a simple ordinary least squares regression of our four outcomes: total sales, bulk sales, café sales, and book sales in Canadian dollars (CAD). This strategy is logically equivalent to taking a simple mean difference between treatment and control. To improve efficiency, the second strategy uses ordinary least squares adjusting for a mean-centered linear time trend as well as mean-centered fixed effects for the day of week, following Lin (2013). In all cases, robust standard errors are used to estimate standard errors, with $p$ values computed under a normal approximation.” p. 4 (PDF p. 4), right column: “In Table 1, we present our estimates of the control means and average treatment effects of the chocolate scent, as computed with ordinary least squares. The direction of the treatment effect on total sales was positive but not statistically significant. None of our estimates of treatment effects are statistically significant at the two-tailed $p$ < .10 level. Our findings are not substantively altered by adjusting for time trends.”
(S5) Table 1, p. 5 (PDF p. 5), as printed. Title: “Table 1 Estimated effects of chocolate scent on bookstore sales”. Columns: “Outcome”, “Unadjusted estimates”, “Adjusted for time trends”. Rows (unadjusted | adjusted). “Total sales”: “Control mean” 575.4 (SE = 34.7) | 593.5 (SE = 30.4); “Treatment effect” 36.6 (SE = 51.6) | 2.7 (SE = 41.7). “Bulk sales”: “Control mean” 72.0 (SE = 13.4) | 71.2 (SE = 16.4); “Treatment effect” 21.8 (SE = 17.5) | 23.2 (SE = 21.2). “Café sales”: “Control mean” 334.7 (SE = 15.2) | 336.5 (SE = 12.6); “Treatment effect” −5.5 (SE = 21.1) | −8.9 (SE = 16.2). “Book sales”: “Control mean” 168.7 (SE = 22.5) | 185.7 (SE = 22.9); “Treatment effect” 20.4 (SE = 32.0) | −11.6 (SE = 32.5). Note under the table: “Estimates of control means and average treatment effects of chocolate scent on total sales, bulk coffee bean/loose tea/spice sales, café sales, and book sales in Canadian dollars. All estimates computed using ordinary least squares regression with robust standard errors. Unadjusted estimates computed without covariates. Adjusted estimates computed using a linear control for the day of experiment and fixed effects for the day of week, all mean-centered”. The table prints no $p$ value; the only $p$ values the article reports are the two of p. 5 (transcribed in P040-T5).
(S6) Replication material; this paragraph is read from the deposited files, not from a page of the article. p. 3 (PDF p. 3), left column: “Full replication data and code are available at the Yale Institution for Social and Policy Studies data archive (http://isps.research.yale.edu/research/data).” The staged archive is staged/code/yale-dataverse-KUKU37-v2.0 (a daily-sales CSV, an R script, the manipulation-check Stata file and its label file). (a) The manipulation-check file has 15 rows and four 0/1 variables with sums notice 6, detect 14, identify 6 and recognize 11; every row with notice = 1 has detect = 1. The ‘detectable ambient scent’ of p. 3 is detection spontaneously or after prompting, the variable detect: 14 of 15. The archive has no code for the interval (.81, 1.06). (b) The sales CSV has $N = 30$ rows, one for each of the days $d$ = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, …, 31 of August (there is no row for day 5), with Treat = 1 on 16 days and Treat = 0 on 14 days; in every row the total equals book + café + bulk. (c) The R script fits, for each of the four outcomes $y$, lm(y ~ Treat) and lm(y ~ Treat + date2 + dowmat), where date2 is the day number minus its mean and dowmat holds the seven indicators of (day number mod 7), each minus its mean. Its helper robust.se multiplies the heteroskedasticity-robust sandwich covariance by (M/(M−1))·((N−1)/(N−K)) with M = N = 30 singleton clusters and K the model rank, which is the factor N/(N−K) (HC1), and passes the result to lmtest::coeftest without a df argument; coeftest then takes the model's residual degrees of freedom and returns Student-$t$ $p$ values (df = Inf would give normal ones). (d) The rows, as ‘day: Treat, book sales, café sales, bulk sales, total sales’ in CAD (columns Treat, Book Tot., cafee, Beans, Grand Tot. of the CSV; every entry is an exact decimal): 1: 0, 181.71, 393.52, 84.2, 659.43; 2: 0, 134.35, 367.57, 81.15, 583.07; 3: 1, 163.55, 293.35, 100.05, 556.95; 4: 0, 85.65, 201.92, 17.05, 304.62; 6: 1, 141.9, 293.21, 102.71, 537.82; 7: 0, 171, 305.03, 69.19, 545.22; 8: 1, 119.9, 420.96, 98.15, 639.01; 9: 1, 267.6, 302.88, 160.35, 730.83; 10: 1, 290.15, 381.19, 172.51, 843.85; 11: 1, 168, 252.55, 19.8, 440.35; 12: 1, 249.05, 296.13, 55.49, 600.67; 13: 0, 225.55, 427.95, 180.31, 833.81; 14: 0, 129.3, 358.84, 160.32, 648.46; 15: 0, 196.4, 341.07, 57.98, 595.45; 16: 1, 200.25, 329.18, 81.02, 610.45; 17: 0, 423.56, 310.92, 32.35, 766.83; 18: 0, 184.75, 246.09, 50.82, 481.66; 19: 1, 178.65, 314.99, 30.8, 524.44; 20: 1, 83.9, 319.55, 122.36, 525.81; 21: 0, 132.35, 362.47, 49.88, 544.7; 22: 1, 112.05, 389, 76.62, 577.67; 23: 1, 120.65, 326.86, 42.45, 489.96; 24: 1, 450.95, 400.49, 151.7, 1003.14; 25: 1, 130.75, 233, 63.05, 426.8; 26: 0, 96.75, 359, 120.13, 575.88; 27: 0, 167.9, 329, 19.05, 515.95; 28: 0, 143.8, 349, 59.91, 552.71; 29: 1, 200, 428.44, 114.12, 742.56; 30: 0, 88.6, 334.07, 24.97, 447.64; 31: 1, 147.6, 286, 108.12, 541.72.
(S7) Audit notation; not in the paper (from the validators' derivations). Binomial model: $n = 15$; for $p \in [0,1]$ and $E \subseteq \{0,\dots,15\}$, $P_p(E) = \sum_{k \in E}  inom{15}{k} p^k (1-p)^{15-k}$ is the law of the number $X$ of customers who detect a scent when the fifteen responses are independent with a common detection probability $p$; the observed count is $x = 14$. Scope of the list. Four candidates are rated errors (ratings.json): P040-E001 (Moderate), P040-E002, P040-E003 and P040-N008 (Minor). Two of them correct mathematical content and are targets: P040-E001 (the interval (.81, 1.06) is used as a 95% lower bound of 80% that it cannot support: counterexample P040-T1, corrected statement P040-T2, passage as printed P040-T3) and P040-E003 (the two printed $p$ values are Student-$t$ values, not the normal-approximation values the Methods name: counterexample P040-T4, corrected statement P040-T5). P040-E002 (31 experimental days against the 30 analysed daily observations) is a finding about data and reporting whose repair is a clarification, and P040-N008 is bibliographic; neither is a target (see error_findings_not_targeted). P040-N001, N002, N006 and N007 are not confirmed, P040-N003, N004 and N005 are undetermined and P040-N009 is out of scope. None of the seven headline claims (candidates.json, P040-H1 to P040-H7) is a mathematical statement: they are empirical estimates, a description of the design and interpretive remarks, so there is no headline_result target; P040-H6 is the claim touched by P040-E001 and P040-H2 the claim touched by P040-E003.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results and discussion, manipulation check: ‘.93 (95 % CI: .81, 1.06)’ and the inference ‘the lower bound of our estimate indicates that at least 80 % of patrons would discern the presence of an ambient scent’; the witness (detection probability 4/5 under a binomial model) is the validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3; headed ‘Page 3 of 6’), right column, paragraph beginning ‘In our sample of 15 customers’
canonical_claim.statement:
An exact witness (validator's construction; not in the paper). Grant the favourable model in which the fifteen responses are independent with a common detection probability $p$. At $p = 4/5$, a value excluded by the printed nominal interval, no deterministic interval rule based on the count that excludes $4/5$ at the observed count can cover with probability $.95$, and the rule that reproduces the printed numbers covers with probability about $.815$.
Setting. $n = 15$; $P_p(X = k) = \binom{15}{k} p^k (1-p)^{15-k}$ for $k = 0,\dots,15$ (standing assumption (S7)); observed count $x = 14$; witness $p_0 = 4/5$.
(A1) $$P_{4/5}(X = 14) = 15\,(4/5)^{14}(1/5) = \frac{3 \cdot 4^{14}}{5^{14}} = \frac{805306368}{6103515625} = 0.13194139533312 > \frac{1}{20}.$$
(A2) Method-free bound. For every map $I$ from $\{0,\dots,15\}$ to subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ with $4/5 \notin I(14)$, $$P_{4/5}\bigl(4/5 \in I(X)\bigr) \le 1 - P_{4/5}(X = 14) = \frac{5298209257}{6103515625} = 0.86805860466688 < \frac{19}{20}.$$ The printed interval $(.81,\ 1.06)$ excludes $4/5$, and so does every interval whose lower endpoint rounds to $.81$ (such an endpoint is at least $.805 > 4/5$). In the same way, for every map $\ell : \{0,\dots,15\} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $\ell(14) > 4/5$, $P_{4/5}\bigl(\ell(X) \le 4/5\bigr) \le \frac{5298209257}{6103515625} < \frac{19}{20}$.
(A3) The rule that reproduces the print. For $k = 0,\dots,15$ put $c_k = k/15$, $r_k = \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{c_k(1-c_k)/15}$ and $I_W(k) = [\,c_k - r_k,\ c_k + r_k\,]$ (the plug-in normal, or Wald, interval with $z = 1.96 = 49/25$). Then: (a) $c_{14} = 14/15$, $c_{14}(1-c_{14})/15 = 14/3375$, $r_{14}^2 = 33614/2109375$, and $$0.8070 < c_{14} - r_{14} < 0.8071, \qquad 1.0595 < c_{14} + r_{14} < 1.0596,$$ so $I_W(14)$ rounds to the printed $(.81,\ 1.06)$, its upper endpoint exceeds $1$, and $4/5 \notin I_W(14)$. (b) $4/5 \in I_W(k)$ if and only if $k \in \{9,10,11,12,13\}$ (equivalently $(4/5 - c_k)^2 \le r_k^2$, a comparison of rationals). (c) $$P_{4/5}\bigl(4/5 \in I_W(X)\bigr) = \sum_{k=9}^{13}\binom{15}{k}(4/5)^k(1/5)^{15-k} = \frac{24866193408}{30517578125} = 0.814815425593344 < \frac{19}{20}.$$ (d) $c_k - r_k \le 4/5$ if and only if $k \le 13$, and $$P_{4/5}\bigl(c_X - r_X \le 4/5\bigr) = 1 - P_{4/5}(X \ge 14) = 1 - \frac{19 \cdot 4^{14}}{5^{15}} = 1 - \frac{5100273664}{30517578125} = \frac{25417304461}{30517578125} = 0.832874232578048 < \frac{19}{20}.$$
(A4) Robustness to the multiplier. (b), (c) and (d) hold unchanged when $49/25$ is replaced by any real $z$ with $19599/10000 \le z \le 19601/10000$; this range contains the normal $.975$ quantile $1.95996\ldots$
Consequence. Under the binomial model the endpoint $.81$ is not a lower confidence bound with confidence $.95$ (nor with confidence $.975$, the one-sided level of an equal-tailed 95% interval): when the true detection probability is exactly $.80$, the rule that produced it puts its lower endpoint above $.80$ with probability $\frac{5100273664}{30517578125} = 0.167125767421952$, and the count $14$ alone, which forces the exclusion of $.80$, has probability $0.13194139533312$. So ‘at least 80 % of patrons’ does not follow at the stated confidence from 14 detections in 15.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: the passage, transcribed in full in P040-T3; ‘a detectable ambient scent’ is detection spontaneously or after prompting (S3), and ‘all but one of the respondents’ gives the count 14 of 15 (confirmed by the deposited file, (S6)(a)). The paper does not say how (.81, 1.06) was computed.
Not in the paper; from the validator (derivation.md, sections 2 to 4): the binomial model $P_p$ of (S7); the witness $p_0 = 4/5$; the reconstruction $I_W$ of the interval, which reproduces the print with $z = 1.96$ and also with the exact normal quantile ($[.807099\ldots,\ 1.059567\ldots]$); coverage of a rule $I$ at $p$, that is $P_p(p \in I(X))$. A deterministic count-based rule is any function of $k \in \{0,\dots,15\}$ alone; (A2) uses nothing else about the rule (no monotonicity, no Wald form). Rounding as in (S7).
canonical_claim.note: Finite-sample calibration counterexamples under an explicitly added independent common-probability binomial model. They reject an exact uniform finite-sample 95% guarantee, not the conventional nominal/asymptotic interpretation of a Wald endpoint, and do not show the true patron rate is below .80.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results and discussion, third paragraph (the manipulation-check estimate, its interval and the inference ‘at least 80 % of patrons’); as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3; headed ‘Page 3 of 6’), right column, paragraph beginning ‘In our sample of 15 customers’
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. “In our sample of 15 customers, six spontaneously detected a scent. Once prompted to consciously attend to scent, all but one of the respondents were able to discern the presence of an ambient scent. Six respondents spontaneously identified that ambient scent as chocolate, and another five reported recognizing the scent as chocolate once the enumerator identified the scent as such. The total proportion of our sample reporting a detectable ambient scent was .93 (95 % CI: .81, 1.06). One limitation of the small sample size in our manipulation check is that the confidence intervals for our estimates are relatively wide. However, since the lower bound of our estimate indicates that at least 80 % of patrons would discern the presence of an ambient scent, we remain confident that the scent was sufficiently detectable.”
Formalizable content of the passage, in the notation of (S7) and P040-T1. (P1) The estimate: $14/15 = 0.9333\ldots$ rounds to the printed $.93$. (P2) The interval: the paper gives no formula; the plug-in normal interval $I_W(14) = 14/15 \pm \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{14/3375}$ has $0.8070 < 14/15 - \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{14/3375} < 0.8071$ and $1.0595 < 14/15 + \tfrac{49}{25}\sqrt{14/3375} < 1.0596$, so it rounds to the printed $(.81,\ 1.06)$; its upper endpoint exceeds $1$. (P1) and (P2) are correct arithmetic. The quoted estimate and reconstructed Wald arithmetic are retained. The lower endpoint has the conventional approximate confidence interpretation; the article does not claim uniform exact finite-sample .95 coverage. The historical exact-coverage proposition and its negation are auxiliary calibration objects under T1, not attributed printed content.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper: the four aspects of the manipulation check and the coding of the responses (S3); ‘a detectable ambient scent’ is detection spontaneously or after prompting, 14 of the 15 customers (‘all but one of the respondents’). The counts in the passage (six spontaneous detections; fourteen detections; six spontaneous identifications; five further recognitions, eleven in all) agree with the deposited file ((S6)(a): 6, 14, 6, 11 of 15). The paper defines neither the interval method nor the population of ‘patrons’, and states no sampling scheme for the fifteen customers.
Not in the paper: the binomial model $P_p$ (S7); the reconstruction $I_W$ of the interval and the rendering (P3) of the inference, which is Sol's natural reading (‘The nominal 95% interval is used to support a confidence-based lower bound of 80% on detection among patrons, with detection defined by the surrounding survey protocol to include spontaneous detection or detection after prompting’), not the paper's wording.
canonical_claim.note: The quoted estimate and reconstructed Wald arithmetic are retained. The lower endpoint has the conventional approximate confidence interpretation; the article does not claim uniform exact finite-sample .95 coverage. The historical exact-coverage proposition and its negation are auxiliary calibration objects under T1, not attributed printed content.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Results and discussion, manipulation check: ‘.93 (95 % CI: .81, 1.06)’ and ‘at least 80 % of patrons’, as repaired by Sol: the exact binomial 95% interval for 14 detections in 15, which contains .80
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3; headed ‘Page 3 of 6’), right column, paragraph beginning ‘In our sample of 15 customers’
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P040-E001, verbatim] “Keep the observed 14 of 15 detections; condition inference on an independent common-probability binomial sampling model, replace the nominal interval with the exact equal-tailed 95% interval [.680515, .998314] (or [.68, 1.00] at the printed precision), and replace the minimum-80%-of-patrons assertion with a statement about the high observed detection rate and its substantial uncertainty. Generalization to patrons requires appropriate sampling assumptions.” Corrected text (validated.json, prior_correction.corrected_text, status ‘correct’), verbatim: “Fourteen of the fifteen surveyed customers reported detecting an ambient scent, either spontaneously or after prompting. Under an independent common-probability binomial sampling model, the exact equal-tailed 95% confidence interval is [.680515, .998314]. The observed detection rate was high, but the small sample does not support a 95% confidence-based lower bound of 80% for patrons; generalization beyond the surveyed customers requires appropriate sampling assumptions.”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Hypothesis (H): the fifteen responses are independent and each customer detects a scent with the same unknown probability $p \in [0,1]$, so that the number $X$ of detections has the law $P_p$ of (S7), $P_p(X = k) = \binom{15}{k}p^k(1-p)^{15-k}$. The observed count is $x = 14$. Definitions: for $k \in \{0,\dots,15\}$ and $p \in [0,1]$ put $$S_k(p) = P_p(X \ge k), \qquad F_k(p) = P_p(X \le k),$$ $$C(k) = \{p \in [0,1] : S_k(p) \ge \tfrac{1}{40} \text{ and } F_k(p) \ge \tfrac{1}{40}\}, \qquad C^{+}(k) = \{p \in [0,1] : S_k(p) \ge \tfrac{1}{20}\}.$$ $C(k)$ is the exact (Clopper–Pearson) equal-tailed 95% confidence set obtained by inverting the two binomial tail tests, and $C^{+}(k)$ is the exact one-sided 95% lower confidence set.
(i) Point estimate. $14/15 = 0.9333\ldots$ rounds to the printed $.93$.
(ii) Tail functions at the observed count. For $p \in [0,1]$: $S_{14}(p) = 15p^{14}(1-p) + p^{15} = p^{14}(15 - 14p)$ and $F_{14}(p) = 1 - p^{15}$. $S_{14}$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,1]$ with $S_{14}(0) = 0$ and $S_{14}(1) = 1$ (its derivative is $210\,p^{13}(1-p) > 0$ on $(0,1)$); $F_{14}$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.
(iii) The interval. There are unique $L, L_{\mathrm{one}} \in (0,1)$ with $S_{14}(L) = 1/40$ and $S_{14}(L_{\mathrm{one}}) = 1/20$, and $U = (39/40)^{1/15}$ is the unique $p \in [0,1]$ with $F_{14}(p) = 1/40$. Then $$C(14) = [L,\ U], \qquad C^{+}(14) = [L_{\mathrm{one}},\ 1].$$
(iv) Numerical values. $$0.680515 < L < 0.680516, \qquad 0.998313 < U < 0.998314, \qquad 0.720603 < L_{\mathrm{one}} < 0.720604;$$ equivalently $S_{14}(680515/10^6) < \tfrac{1}{40} < S_{14}(680516/10^6)$, $(998313/10^6)^{15} < \tfrac{39}{40} < (998314/10^6)^{15}$ and $S_{14}(720603/10^6) < \tfrac{1}{20} < S_{14}(720604/10^6)$. To six decimals the interval is $[.680515,\ .998314]$; at the paper's two-decimal precision it is $[.68,\ 1.00]$, against the printed $(.81,\ 1.06)$.
(v) The threshold of 80% is not excluded. $$S_{14}(4/5) = \frac{19 \cdot 4^{14}}{5^{15}} = \frac{5100273664}{30517578125} = 0.167125767421952 > \frac{1}{20} > \frac{1}{40}, \qquad F_{14}(4/5) = 1 - (4/5)^{15} = \frac{29443836301}{30517578125} \ge \frac{1}{40}.$$ Hence $4/5 \in C(14)$ and $4/5 \in C^{+}(14)$, that is, $L < L_{\mathrm{one}} < 4/5$: neither the equal-tailed exact 95% interval nor the one-sided exact 95% lower bound supports $p \ge .80$, and the exact one-sided test of $p \le 4/5$ against $p > 4/5$ at the count 14 has $p$ value $0.167125767421952$.
(vi) What makes ‘95%’ true of the replacement. Under (H), for every $p \in [0,1]$, $$P_p\bigl(p \in C(X)\bigr) \ge \frac{19}{20} \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_p\bigl(p \in C^{+}(X)\bigr) \ge \frac{19}{20}.$$ (For fixed $p$, the set $\{k : S_k(p) < 1/40\}$ is an upper set of counts and has $P_p$-probability below $1/40$; the set $\{k : F_k(p) < 1/40\}$ is a lower set of counts and has $P_p$-probability below $1/40$; likewise with $1/20$ for $C^{+}$.) By P040-T1 (A2) no deterministic count-based rule that excludes $4/5$ at $k = 14$ has this property.
What the corrected statement does not assert: that the detection probability is below $.80$, that the scent was not detectable, or anything about patrons beyond the fifteen surveyed customers without a sampling assumption that makes (H) describe them.

canonical_claim.statement:
An exact witness (validator's recalculation from the deposited data; not in the paper): for the two regressions whose $p$ values the article prints, the normal-approximation $p$ value named in the Methods does not round to the printed number.
Setting. Notation of standing assumption (S7); the 30 rows of (S6)(d); the adjusted design $X^{a}$ ($N = 30$, $K = 9$, $\nu = 21$); $p_N(q) = 2(1 - \Phi(\sqrt q))$.
(B1) Café sales (outcome: the café column). $$\hat\beta_T = -\frac{146561}{16484}, \qquad v = \frac{42131842162249950707521}{161509653387533360000}, \qquad q_{\text{café}} = \frac{\hat\beta_T^2}{v} = \frac{12767624825803755635000}{42131842162249950707521}.$$ In decimals $\hat\beta_T \approx -8.891107$ and $\sqrt v \approx 16.151244$, which round to the entries $-8.9$ (SE = 16.2) of Table 1; $q_{\text{café}} \approx 0.303040$, $\sqrt{q_{\text{café}}} \approx 0.550491$.
(B2) Bulk sales (outcome: the bulk column). $$\hat\beta_T = \frac{955199}{41210}, \qquad v = \frac{10415886991743115636339}{23072807626790480000}, \qquad q_{\text{bulk}} = \frac{\hat\beta_T^2}{v} = \frac{12396039010057804992800}{10415886991743115636339}.$$ In decimals $\hat\beta_T \approx 23.178816$ and $\sqrt v \approx 21.247014$, which round to the entries $23.2$ (SE = 21.2) of Table 1; $q_{\text{bulk}} \approx 1.190109$, $\sqrt{q_{\text{bulk}}} \approx 1.090921$.
(B3) $0.58198 < p_N(q_{\text{café}}) < 0.58199$. This lies strictly inside $(0.575,\ 0.585)$, so the normal-approximation $p$ value rounds to $.58$ and not to the printed $.59$.
(B4) $0.27530 < p_N(q_{\text{bulk}}) < 0.27531$. This lies strictly inside $(0.275,\ 0.285)$, so the normal-approximation $p$ value rounds to $.28$ and not to the printed $.29$.
Consequence. The sentence ‘with $p$ values computed under a normal approximation’ is false of both $p$ values that the article prints: neither $.59$ nor $.29$ is the two-decimal rounding of $2(1 - \Phi(|\hat\beta_T|/\sqrt v))$ for the regression it is attached to. (They are the Student-$t$ values with 21 degrees of freedom: P040-T5.)

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Methods, ‘with p values computed under a normal approximation’, as repaired by Sol: the p values use a Student-t reference distribution with the residual degrees of freedom (28 unadjusted, 21 adjusted), under which the printed p = .59 and p = .29 are correct

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; p. 4, left column] “In all cases, robust standard errors are used to estimate standard errors, with $p$ values computed under a normal approximation.” [Printed; p. 5, left column] “The direction of the treatment effect on café sales was slightly negative, though not statistically significant (average estimated decrease of 8.9CAD from a control average of 336.5CAD, two-tailed $p$ = .59) and the direction of treatment on bulk coffee bean/loose tea/spice sales was slightly positive, though not statistically significant (average estimated increase of 23.2CAD from a control average of 71.2CAD, two-tailed $p$ = .29).”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P040-E003, verbatim] “Replace 'under a normal approximation' with 'using a Student-t reference distribution with the model's residual degrees of freedom (28 for the unadjusted regressions and 21 for the adjusted regressions)'. Alternatively retain the normal-reference description, specify df = Inf in coeftest, and change the two printed p-values to .58 and .28.” Under the first branch the Methods sentence reads (prior_correction.corrected_text, status ‘correct’, verbatim): “In all cases, robust standard errors are used to estimate standard errors, with p values computed using a Student-t reference distribution with the model's residual degrees of freedom (28 for the unadjusted regressions and 21 for the adjusted regressions).”
[Mathematical content, with every hypothesis] Notation of (S7); the 30 rows of (S6)(d); for each outcome and each design, $\hat\beta_T$, $v$, $q = \hat\beta_T^2/v$ and $\nu = N - K$ as defined there; $p_T(q;\nu) = 1 - 2\int_0^{\sqrt q} f_\nu(t)\,dt$ is the two-tailed Student-$t$ $p$ value.
(i) Degrees of freedom. $N = 30$. $X^{u}$ has rank $2$, so $\nu = 28$ for each unadjusted regression. The ten columns $1$, $T$, $d - \bar d$ and the seven centred indicators $\mathbf{1}\{d \bmod 7 = c\} - n_c/30$ ($c = 0,\dots,6$) have rank $9$: the seven centred indicators sum to zero in every row, and the nine columns of $X^{a}$ are linearly independent. So $\nu = 21$ for each adjusted regression.
(ii) The two printed values. With $q_{\text{café}}$ and $q_{\text{bulk}}$ the exact squared statistics of the adjusted regressions (P040-T4 (B1), (B2)) and $f_{21}(t) = \frac{4^{10}}{\pi\binom{20}{10}\sqrt{21}}\,(1 + t^2/21)^{-11}$: $$0.58779 < p_T(q_{\text{café}};\,21) < 0.58780,$$ which lies strictly inside $(0.585,\ 0.595)$ and rounds to the printed $.59$; and $$0.28766 < p_T(q_{\text{bulk}};\,21) < 0.28767,$$ which lies strictly inside $(0.285,\ 0.295)$ and rounds to the printed $.29$.
(iii) The significance statement under the corrected reference. For the eight regressions of Table 1 the exact squared statistics $q$ are: unadjusted total $263679812816672/522999591200175$ ($\approx 0.504168$); unadjusted bulk $23273498735648/15141092298015$ ($\approx 1.537108$); unadjusted café $1492978176032/21949506186495$ ($\approx 0.068019$); unadjusted book $9067019347232/22381571766655$ ($\approx 0.405111$); adjusted total $1200277903320876335774/280628848000463708694463$ ($\approx 0.004277$); adjusted bulk $12396039010057804992800/10415886991743115636339$ ($\approx 1.190109$); adjusted café $12767624825803755635000/42131842162249950707521$ ($\approx 0.303040$); adjusted book $3084161273413343448962/24391999904970062376441$ ($\approx 0.126442$). Each is at most the unadjusted-bulk value, which is below $8/5$. For each of the eight, $p_T(q;\nu) > 1/10$ with its own $\nu$ ($28$ unadjusted, $21$ adjusted), and also $p_N(q) > 1/10$. The smallest values are those of unadjusted bulk sales: $$0.22533 < p_T(q;\,28) < 0.22534 \qquad\text{and}\qquad 0.21504 < p_N(q) < 0.21505.$$ So the sentence of p. 4, ‘None of our estimates of treatment effects are statistically significant at the two-tailed $p$ < .10 level’, holds under the corrected Student-$t$ reference and under the normal reference alike.
(iv) Alternative branch of the repair. If the normal-reference description is kept, the two printed values become $.58$ and $.28$: this is P040-T4 (B3), (B4).
What the corrected statement does not assert: that the robust $t$ statistic has an exact Student-$t$ distribution under the null hypothesis, or that either reference gives a test of exact size; Student-$t$ is named as the reference distribution that was used.
